title: Rex, the little dinosaur
summary: Rex is the smallest in his family, and he has a roar so enormous it embarrasses him. So he holds it in. And holding it in gives him hiccups.

scenes.text:
A very, very long time ago, in a valley full of giant ferns, Rex lived with his family.

His family was huge. His dad was so big he blocked out the sun. His mum could eat the leaves off the tops of trees without stretching. And when they all walked together, the ground shook with their footsteps.

Rex was the smallest. Shorter than a fern. Lighter than a big stone.

But he had a secret.

He had an enormous roar. Bigger than his dad's. Bigger than anyone's.

He had used it just once, when he was very little. The whole herd jumped, a bird fell off its branch, and Grandma choked on a fern.

And then everyone laughed and laughed.

From that day on, Rex never let out a single roar.

When something made him cross, he held it in. When something made him happy, he held that in too. He pressed his mouth shut tight and kept it all inside.

The trouble is, a roar that big doesn't fit inside such a small dinosaur.

So it came out as hiccups.

"Hic!"

Strange hiccups, with a little growl at the end.

"Hic-grrr!"

His brothers and sisters covered their mouths so they wouldn't giggle. And Rex turned even greener with embarrassment.

One morning, the herd set off for the big river.

To get there they had to cross a gorge: a narrow path between two towering walls of rock. The grown-ups went in front, chatting away, making the ground shake. Rex came behind, hopping from stone to stone.

That's why he was the first to see it.

High up on the wall, a pebble came loose and rolled down. Then another. Then a whole lot of them, with a dry little clatter.

The wall was crumbling. And his family was walking straight towards it.

"Look out!" shouted Rex.

But his normal voice was tiny. Nobody turned round.

Rex knew there was only one thing they would all hear.

The thing he had been keeping in for so long.

He breathed in until he was full right up, opened his mouth as wide as it would go, and roared.

The roar bounced off the walls of the gorge. The birds flew away. Even the clouds seemed to stop and listen.

The whole herd froze on the spot.

And just in front of them, in the exact place they had been about to walk, the rocks came down with a crash.

The dust settled slowly. For a long while, nobody said a word.

It was Grandma who came over first.

She lowered her enormous head until it was level with Rex's, and looked at him for a long time.

"That roar," she said at last, "isn't for frightening anyone."

Rex waited for her to laugh. But Grandma didn't laugh.

"It's for warning us," she said. "And you've just saved us all."

Since that day, whenever the herd sets off, Rex walks in front. The smallest of them all, leading the way. And if he ever sees something the others don't, he knows exactly what to do.

Oh. And the hiccups never came back.
